cover.headline: The clean-up worked, the returns problem did not go away: a ~13% ROE rural lender facing a drought year, priced about right
cover.lead: M&M Finance, the Mahindra group's rural lender (group AUM ₹1.46 lakh cr: cars and utility vehicles, commercial vehicles, used vehicles, tractors, plus small-business and housing loans), has finished a three-year clean-up: Stage 3 loans 3.45% (9.0% in FY21), Stage 2+3 at an eight-year low of 8.3%, credit cost 1.5% of assets and Q1FY27 profit up 75%. The street values it on **P/B (1.8-2.0x FY28E book)** and expects ROE to reach ~15%. We are more cautious: the 2026 monsoon ended ~13% below normal, IRDAI wants to cap the insurance commissions that lifted fee income, and growing 14-15% a year while paying out 36% of profit pushes leverage up and margins down. We forecast EPS of ₹25.5 / ₹27.0 / ₹31.5 for FY27-29E and ROE of 12.5-13.4%. Applying **1.4x to Sep-28E book of ₹235** (its own 1.4x median forward P/B since 2021, adjusted for the sector's −6.4% move and for its higher level since 2023, ×1.07) gives **{{dcf.tp|inr}} ({{dcf.upside|chg}}): we initiate with HOLD**. P/E gives ₹351; the intrinsic cross-checks are lower (justified P/B ₹246, residual income ₹241): the price already assumes a ~{{dcf.impliedRoe|pct0}} long-run ROE. Bull {{scen.bull.tp|inr}}; bear {{scen.bear.tp|inr}}.

arguments.p: Stage 3 fell from 9.0% of loans in FY21 to 3.45% in Jun-2026 and Stage 2+3 from over 10% to 8.32%; collection efficiency holds at 95-98%; provision cover is 58.1% with ₹852 cr of management overlays on top. The whole vehicle-loan business now runs on a digital stack (Udaan) with a flat headcount of ~22,600. Q1FY27 delivered a 2.4% ROA and 14.3% ROE (standalone), the best since FY19.

arguments.h: But returns are still structurally low
arguments.p: ROE has been 6-12% for seven years, below a ~13.4% cost of equity. The 2022 "Vision 2025" promised a 2.5% ROA, 7.5% NIM and 2x AUM; FY25 delivered 1.9%, 6.5% and 1.84x. The new FY31 aim (ROA 2.2-2.5%) gives a 13-15% ROE at the planned 6x leverage: about the cost of equity, not far above it. We model {{F.roe.0|pct}} / {{F.roe.1|pct}} / {{F.roe.2|pct}}.

The monsoon ended ~13% below normal, the fourth-weakest since 2001 (tractors are 12% of AUM; after the back-to-back deficient monsoons of 2014-15, profit fell 43% by FY17). IRDAI's 23-Sep consultation would cap loan-linked insurance commission; M&M Finance earned ₹507 cr of insurance commission in FY26, 13.3% of pre-tax profit. And a repo hike was expected in October. The stock fell 20% from its August high.

At ₹324.85 the stock trades at 1.44x our FY28E book and 12.0x FY28E EPS, in line with its 1.4x median forward P/B since 2021. Our 1.4x Sep-28E book gives {{dcf.tp|inr}}, below the street's median ₹410: we see less ROE improvement than the brokers (FY28E ROE {{F.roe.1|pct}} vs their 13-15%). We would buy below ~₹285.

catalysts: Q2FY27 results (due by mid-November 2026): the first read of the weak monsoon on tractor and rural collections; Q2 is seasonally soft and Q1 pulled tractor buying forward.
IRDAI's insurance-distribution reforms: consultation paper of 23-Sep-2026, comments due 25-Oct-2026; caps of ~2-5% on loan-linked commission would cut fee income.
RBI's October 2026 policy: most economists polled expected a 25bp repo hike; 44% of M&M Finance's borrowings are floating-rate.
The ₹852 cr management overlays: built "specifically" for a compromised monsoon; using them would protect FY27 profit (worth ~₹4.6 a share after tax if released in full).
MRHFL merger: board approval on 5-Aug-2026, effective 1-Apr-2027 subject to NCLT, RBI and NHB approval; mortgages move into the parent.

sections.title: A rural vehicle lender with 1,300 branches, half its book on Mahindra vehicles

blocks.p: Mahindra & Mahindra Financial Services (M&M Finance, MMFSL) is the lending arm of the Mahindra group; Mahindra & Mahindra (M&M) owns 52.5%. It is an upper-layer, deposit-taking NBFC (the RBI's tier for the largest non-bank lenders), rated AAA by CRISIL, India Ratings and CARE. It makes money the way every lender does: in FY26 it borrowed at ~7.2% (our measure), lent at ~13.7%, earned another ~1.9% of loans in fees (insurance commission, loan fees and its insurance-broking subsidiary's income), and kept what was left after operating costs (~4.3% of loans, incl. the broking subsidiary's payouts) and loan losses (~1.8%). In FY26 interest income was ₹18,428 cr of ₹21,005 cr of consolidated revenue.

Its customers are farmers, small transport operators, self-employed buyers of cars and small trucks, and small businesses in villages and small towns: 1,348 offices, 6,000+ dealers, 95% of India's pin codes and over 12 million customers served since inception (about 2.4 million live). Vehicles ("wheels") are 88% of MMFSL's ₹1,37,449 cr book (Jun-2026) and 46% of the book is financed Mahindra vehicles (tractors, utility vehicles, pick-ups). Housing sits in a subsidiary, Mahindra Rural Housing Finance (MRHFL, ₹8,976 cr of loans), which the board approved merging into the parent from Apr-2027.

blocks.callout: **Why this matters:** M&M Finance is two things at once. It is the in-house financier for Mahindra's tractors and utility vehicles, which gives it volume, dealer access and a brand rural buyers trust; and it is an ordinary rural lender competing with banks, Shriram, Chola and HDB for the same borrowers. Management insists the M&M link is "earned, not given": there are no special scorecards for Mahindra customers. The flip side of a rural, vehicle-heavy book is cyclicality: when the monsoon fails or a fleet operator's diesel bill jumps, M&M Finance's borrowers feel it first.

sections.title: Three equity raises, two clean-ups and one missed vision in nine years

blocks.p: M&M Finance was set up in 1991 to finance Mahindra vehicles and listed in 2006. Its history since FY18 is a cycle: raise equity, grow fast, hit a rural or funding shock, clean up the book, repeat. It raised equity in FY18 (QIP plus a preferential issue to M&M), in the Covid year (a 1-for-1 rights issue at ₹50) and again in June 2025 (1-for-8 at ₹194). In between came the IL&FS liquidity crunch of 2018-19, Covid, an RBI ban on outsourced recovery, a branch fraud and two changes in how provisions are calculated. The current team (Raul Rebello, CEO since Apr-2024) inherited a cleaned-up book and has spent two years rebuilding systems.

sections.title: Vehicle demand was strong in Q1; then the monsoon failed, rates turned and IRDAI moved

blocks.p: M&M Finance's book rides on rural India's vehicle cycle, and FY27 started well. Tractor disbursements rose 45% in Q1FY27: delayed rains stretched the pre-sowing buying season and the rabi harvest had left farmers with cash (CEO, 21-Jul). Rural car and utility-vehicle sales grew faster than urban ones, helped by the cut in GST rates on small cars and tractors in Sep-2025, and management gained lender market share in every vehicle category except commercial vehicles. Heavy trucks and construction equipment for large fleets have moved to banks, which fund themselves more cheaply; M&M Finance is deliberately shrinking there.

Then the season turned. The IMD had forecast a below-normal monsoon from April (92% of the long-period average, cut to 90% in May) because of El Niño, and the season ended on 30-Sep-2026 about 12.6-13% short, the fourth-weakest since 2001, with the East and North-East driest and Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh and Gujarat also short in July. Low soil moisture and reservoirs now threaten rabi sowing. For a lender whose tractor borrowers often repay twice a year from harvests, this is the main FY27 risk: management built overlays in Q3 and Q4 of FY26 "specifically" for a compromised monsoon, and slowed growth in vulnerable segments by asking for higher down-payments.

The money side also turned less friendly. September 2026 was a bad month for Indian markets: the Nifty fell ~5% by 28-Sep on foreign selling, Brent was ~$106, US 10-year yields 5.2%, and most economists polled expected the RBI to raise the repo rate by 25bp to 5.5% in October. M&M Finance is AAA-rated and part-funded by public deposits, but 44% of its borrowings are floating-rate and its cost of funds already rose ~10bp in Q1. Among listed lenders it is mid-sized (₹45,114 cr market value on 30-Sep-2026) and the least profitable large vehicle financier: FY26 ROE 11.9% and ROA 1.89%, against 19.3% / 2.34% at Chola and 16.4% / 3.26% at Shriram.

blocks.callout: **Our view:** demand is not M&M Finance's problem in a normal year: rural vehicle demand is healthy and it is the largest tractor financier in India. Its problems are the ones a rural lender cannot diversify away: **the monsoon** (which drives tractor, rural-transport and small-business cash flows), **price competition from banks** in the safer segments, and **the cost of servicing small rural borrowers** (high branch and collection costs). This year two more have joined: dearer money and regulation of the insurance income that had become its fastest-growing revenue line.

blocks.callout: **Our view:** the tailwinds that lifted FY26 and Q1FY27 (tractor demand, GST cuts, falling funding costs and fast-growing insurance fees) were cyclical or are now under threat; the structural ones (digital productivity, mortgages and SME) are real but slow. That is why we model ROE of only {{F.roe.0|pct}} in FY27E and {{F.roe.1|pct}} in FY28E, even after a 75% jump in Q1 profit.

sections.title: Growth is ~12% in vehicles and ~30% elsewhere; the mix will shift, slowly

blocks.p: MMFSL disbursed ₹61,118 cr in FY26 (+6%) and ₹15,564 cr in Q1FY27 (+22%). Group AUM grew 13% in FY26 to ₹{{fin.aum.11|num}} cr and the standalone book 13% in the year to Jun-2026. Management now describes the plan in two parts: the wheels business (83% of group AUM) should grow at about the vehicle market, ~11-12% a year, while the non-wheels businesses (SME, personal loans, leasing and housing, 17%) compound at 30% or more, for a 16-18% group CAGR over FY26-31. In Q1FY27 wheels AUM grew ~11-12% and non-wheels ~28-30%, exactly on that plan. The problem is arithmetic: with 83% of the book growing at 11-12%, the group grows ~14-15% for the next two or three years, and the 16-18% only arrives late in the period, if at all.

blocks.p: Vehicle finance is the core: ~₹1.2 lakh cr of AUM in Jun-2026 and 92% of FY26 disbursements. The mix tells the strategy. Passenger vehicles (41.5% of the book) are mostly utility vehicles and entry-level cars for rural and semi-urban buyers; M&M Finance "sits out" premium-car loans where banks price at very low returns, and lost unit share there in FY26. Commercial vehicles and construction equipment (19.2%, down from 22.9% in FY24) are being re-shaped away from large fleet operators, who now borrow from banks, toward small and light trucks. Tractors (12.4%, up from 10.7%) are where it leads: management calls it "the number 1 tractor financier in the country by a fair margin", with separate teams for Mahindra and Swaraj tractors. Used vehicles (12.3%) carry the highest yields.

blocks.callout: **Our view:** the wheels franchise is a real asset (deep dealer reach, the Mahindra link, 30 years of rural repayment data), but it does not earn high returns. Yields have fallen as banks and well-funded NBFCs compete for the better borrowers, so M&M Finance's growth leans on tractors and used vehicles, where risk is higher and the monsoon matters most. sections.kicker: Segment: SME, housing, insurance broking (17% of AUM)
sections.title: Non-wheels: growing 30%, but from a small base; insurance broking is a hidden profit pool

blocks.p: The diversification has three legs. **SME loans** (6.2% of MMFSL's book; ~₹8,500 cr) to small businesses, dealers and supply-chain partners grew 32% in FY26; management wants faster growth but calls it "still capability building". **Housing** sits in MRHFL (₹8,976 cr of loans, Jun-2026), which lost ₹228 cr in FY25 while it wrote down a legacy rural book (Stage 3 from 9.0% to 2.4%) and has since returned to profit (₹30 cr in Q1FY27) and growth (disbursements +128%); it merges into the parent from Apr-2027, which lets the NBFC branches sell home loans and loans against property directly. **Personal loans and leasing** to existing customers are the third leg ("others", 5.3%).

The fee businesses matter as much. The corporate insurance agency (licensed in FY25) earned ₹507 cr of commission in FY26, 2.4x FY25. Mahindra Insurance Brokers (MIBL, 100%) placed ₹4,590 cr of premium and earned ₹114 cr of profit in FY26 (₹38 cr in Q1FY27, +83%), motor insurance in the Mahindra ecosystem plus open-market, commercial-lines and reinsurance business; it pays regular dividends to the parent. The AMC joint venture (51%) turned profitable in FY26. Together these lifted fee income from 0.8% of AUM in FY23 to 1.9% in FY26, the main reason ROA reached 2%.

They cannot change group ROE quickly. The fee businesses can, in both directions: IRDAI's proposed caps on loan-linked insurance commission (23-Sep-2026) put the fastest-growing income line at risk. Management said in July that its products are "very clean" and it does not expect "a very big departure" in fee income; we cut ~0.13% of AUM from FY28E anyway.

sections.title: Margins recovered in FY26 on cheaper money and fees; leverage and IRDAI now push the other way

blocks.p: M&M Finance reports a "NIM" that is really its gross spread: total income including fees, less interest cost, over average assets. On that basis it fell from 6.8% in FY24 to 6.5% in FY25 and recovered to 7.1% in FY26 and 7.3% in Q1FY27. The recovery did not come from lending rates, which kept falling (loan income 11.7% of assets in FY25, 11.6% in FY26, 11.5% in Q1FY27): it came from cheaper funding (interest cost 6.3% → 5.8%, helped by RBI cuts and the June-2025 rights issue) and from fees (1.1% → 1.5%). On our basis (interest income only, over average group AUM) NIM was {{fin.nim.9|pct}}, {{fin.nim.10|pct}} and {{fin.nim.11|pct}} in FY24-26, and the yield on AUM fell from {{fin.yieldOnAum.8|pct}} in FY23 to {{fin.yieldOnAum.11|pct}} in FY26.

blocks.p: **Two things squeeze our forecast margin.** First, **leverage**: at a 36% payout and ~13% ROE, equity grows ~8% a year, so 14-15% AUM growth must be funded with more debt; borrowings rise from 4.8x to {{fin.debtEquity.14|n2}}x equity by FY29E and NIM drifts from {{F.nim.0|pct}} (FY27E) to {{F.nim.2|pct}} (FY29E) even with yields flat. Second, **fees**: of ₹2,577 cr of FY26 fee and other income, ₹507 cr (0.38% of AUM) was insurance commission (life ₹315 cr, mostly credit-linked; general ₹192 cr) and ₹1,456 cr MIBL's broking income. IRDAI's 23-Sep-2026 paper would cap loan-linked commission at ~2-5%; the company has not said how much of its commission is loan-linked (gap). Seasonality is smaller too: Stage 2 rose 11bp from March to June 2026 against 41bp a year earlier. Credit cost (company basis) was 1.3% of assets in FY25, 1.7% in FY26 including overlays, and 1.5% in Q1FY27 against 1.9% a year earlier. Management guides to 1.3-1.7% through the cycle.

sections.title: Funding: AAA, deposit-taking and well-buffered; an advantage over most NBFCs, not over banks

blocks.p: MMFSL owed ₹1,25,979 cr at face value in Jun-2026 (standalone). Half was bank and financial-institution loans, a fifth NCDs, 11% public fixed deposits (₹13,719 cr; 88,550+ active depositors in FY26), 9.5% securitisation and assignment, and the rest offshore loans and commercial paper. It is rated AAA by CRISIL, India Ratings and CARE, a notch above Chola (AA+), helped by Mahindra parentage. 44% of borrowings are floating-rate. On our measure the group paid {{fin.costOfFunds.11|pct}} on its borrowings in FY26, down from {{fin.costOfFunds.10|pct}} in FY25 (Chola: ~7.45%).

blocks.callout: **Why it matters:** NBFCs fail on liquidity before they fail on credit, and M&M Finance learned that in 2018-19, when the IL&FS default froze wholesale funding and its profit fell 42% in FY20. Today it holds ₹14,650 cr of cash and liquid investments, including ~₹5,000 cr of extra buffer built against the West Asia and monsoon risks, against ₹24,832 cr of borrowings maturing in the six months to Dec-2026, plus undrawn bank lines. The extra buffer has a cost (the CEO tied most of Q1's ~25bp fall in loan income ÷ assets to it; the CFO called it mainly a denominator effect) and management will release it when conditions settle. Funding is a modest edge over AA-rated peers, not over banks.

sections.title: Capital: plenty today, but three raises in nine years and EPS barely above FY19

blocks.p: Capital adequacy was 18.5% in Jun-2026 (Tier 1 16.5%) against RBI minimums of 15% and 10%, and debt was 5.0x equity. Management says it will not need capital for "at least 6 to 8 quarters" and is comfortable taking debt ÷ equity to "6-plus". Our model agrees: at 14-15% AUM growth and a 36% payout, AUM ÷ equity rises from {{fin.leverage.11|n2}}x to {{fin.leverage.14|n2}}x by FY29E without new equity.

The longer record is less comfortable. M&M Finance has raised equity three times since FY18, ₹8,196 cr in all, and the share count has gone from ~57 cr (FY17) to 139.0 cr. Net worth grew 16% a year over FY17-26, but book value per share only ~11% a year, and EPS of ₹20.54 in FY26 is just +17% above FY19's ₹17.55 (2.3% a year). Shareholders have funded growth that has not yet earned its cost of equity.

blocks.callout: **Value trap or not?** A value trap looks cheap and stays cheap because returns never improve. M&M Finance is not cheap on fundamentals: at a 13.4% cost of equity and ~13% ROE, it is worth ~1.1x book (our justified P/B), and it trades at 1.70x FY26 book. Returns have improved (ROA 2.0% in FY26 vs 1.7% in FY24; 2.4% in Q1FY27) and the transformation is real. But getting from ~13% to the ~15% the most bullish brokers model (Emkay 14.9% FY28E, 15.6% FY29E) needs credit cost at the bottom of the range, no IRDAI damage and further cost cuts, all at once, in a drought year. Our answer: not a trap at this price, but no bargain either; the stock already pays for a good part of the turnaround.

sections.title: Ten years, three collapses: profit has never compounded for long

blocks.p: M&M Finance's consolidated profit was ₹925 cr in FY15 and ₹2,861 cr in FY26: about 11% a year, but the path was anything but smooth. Profit fell 15% in FY16 and 33% in FY17 (two droughts in a row hit rural borrowers), recovered to a record ₹1,867 cr in FY19, then fell 42% in FY20 and 28% more in FY21 (the IL&FS funding squeeze, then Covid), and only passed the FY19 peak in FY23. Since then it has grown in fits: −6% in FY24 (vehicle-finance losses and the Aizawl fraud), +16% in FY25 (helped by a provision release) and +27% in FY26. Return on equity has been between 6% and 12% in every year since FY20, below the 13-14% cost of equity in all of them.

blocks.callout: **Our view:** this is a cyclical, not a compounding, franchise. The good news is that the last two years have been the cleanest in a decade: credit cost back inside the 1.3-1.7% band, Stage 3 down to 3.4%, and profit up 75% in Q1FY27. The bad news is that even the good years have produced only ~12% ROE, because margins have been squeezed by competition in vehicle loans and costs are high. We forecast EPS of {{F.eps.0|n2}} / {{F.eps.1|n2}} / {{F.eps.2|n2}} for FY27-29E and ROE of {{F.roe.0|pct}} / {{F.roe.1|pct}} / {{F.roe.2|pct}}: better than history, still around the cost of equity.

sections.title: Competitive advantage: a real rural franchise that has never earned high returns

blocks.p: A lender's moat shows up as a lasting gap between what it earns on loans and what it pays for money, costs and losses. M&M Finance has the ingredients (reach, a captive vehicle maker, AAA funding) but not the outcome: its ROE has been 6-12% for seven years and its ROA on assets (1.89% in FY26) is the lowest of the large vehicle financiers. We test each source of advantage.

sections.title: Earnings quality: clean audits, but provisions have been the swing factor in three years out of three

blocks.p: We rate accounting **AMBER**. Joint auditors M M Nissim & Co and M.P. Chitale & Co gave an unmodified opinion on FY26, and disclosure is good (stage-wise provisions, an IRACP comparison, a credit-cost split between provisions and write-offs). But reported profit has been shaped by provisioning decisions in each of the last three years:

bullets: **ECL model refreshes (every Q3).** In Q3FY25 the refresh released ₹434 cr of provisions and Stage 3 cover fell from 63% to 51%, flattering FY25 profit (+16%). In Q3FY26 the refresh would have released provisions again; management parked the release as a ₹635 cr "management overlay" instead. That was prudent, but it means the overlay is partly a re-labelled model release that can come back into profit.

**₹852 cr of overlays** (₹635 cr Q3FY26 + ₹217 cr Q4FY26), 0.6% of AUM, explicitly built for "a possible compromised monsoon". If FY27-28 stress is absorbed by releasing them, reported credit cost will look better than the underlying loss rate; a full release is worth ~₹4.6 a share after tax. We assume no release.

**Write-offs have not fallen much.** End losses (write-offs) were ₹1,715 cr, ₹1,559 cr and ₹1,959 cr in FY24-26 (1.6%, 1.2% and 1.4% of assets) while Stage 3 fell from 4.5% (FY23) to 3.4%; the year-to-year swings in credit cost came mostly from provisions (+₹108 cr, +₹59 cr, +₹482 cr, standalone).

**One-offs.** The new labour codes cost ₹133 cr (Q3FY26, exceptional; Screener shows it inside other income). The Aizawl branch fraud (₹136 cr, FY24: forged KYC on ~2,900 loans with staff collusion) was fully provided and written off in Q3FY26; the company says it found no similar fraud elsewhere.

**Fee optics.** Standalone fee income includes dividends from MIBL (eliminated on consolidation); consolidated fees include MIBL's gross broking income (₹1,456 cr) with payouts in opex (₹1,318 cr of fees and commission expense), which inflates both lines. Non-interest-bearing trade advances to dealers swing AUM and yields between Q2 and Q3.

blocks.callout: **Read this right:** a lender's operating cash flow is negative whenever its loan book grows, because new loans count as an operating outflow. What matters is whether equity keeps up with the book. M&M Finance pays out ~36% of profit, so at a 12-13% ROE its equity grows only ~8% a year from retained profit. At our 14-15% AUM growth, AUM ÷ equity rises from {{fin.leverage.11|n2}}x (FY26) to {{fin.leverage.14|n2}}x (FY29E) and borrowings ÷ equity to {{fin.debtEquity.14|n2}}x, inside the "6-plus" the CFO is comfortable with. sections.title: Our honest summary: a better lender, a HOLD at this price

blocks.callout: **What you are buying:** India's largest tractor financier and Mahindra's in-house lender, with a 1,300-branch rural franchise, AAA funding and a strong parent; a book cleaned up to its best asset quality in eight years (Stage 3 3.45%, Stage 2+3 8.32%, ₹852 cr of overlays on top); a finished digital rebuild; and profit up 75% in Q1FY27. You are also buying a lender whose ROE has not beaten its cost of equity since FY19 and whose profit fell 28-42% in three of the last ten years.

**What you are paying:** 1.44x our FY28E book and 12.0x FY28E EPS, in line with its 1.4x median forward P/B since 2021 after a 20% fall from the August high. On the street's method that gives {{dcf.tp|inr}} ({{dcf.upside|chg}}) and a HOLD. It is not cheap on fundamentals: at a 13.4% cost of equity a ~13% ROE lender is worth ~1.1x book (justified P/B ₹246, residual income ₹241), and the price implies a ~{{dcf.impliedRoe|pct0}} long-run ROE. You are paying for the turnaround to keep working through a drought year.

exhibit.title: Terms used in this report
head: Term
What it means
rows: Non-banking financial company: an RBI-regulated lender without a banking licence. The "upper layer" is the RBI's tier for the largest NBFCs, with bank-like rules. A deposit-taking NBFC may accept public fixed deposits (not current or savings accounts).
Mahindra & Mahindra Financial Services (the listed lender); Mahindra Rural Housing Finance (98.43% housing subsidiary, merging in); Mahindra Insurance Brokers (100% insurance broker).

MMFSL's loans including provisions (₹1,37,449 cr, Jun-2026); group AUM adds MRHFL's loans. Wheels = vehicle loans (cars, trucks, used vehicles, tractors, three-wheelers); non-wheels = SME, personal loans, leasing and housing.
Net interest income = interest earned − interest paid. Our NIM = NII ÷ average AUM. The company's "NIM" is its gross spread: total income incl. fees, less interest, ÷ average assets.
NII plus fees and other operating income; operating expenses ÷ net total income.
Provisions ÷ average AUM (our basis) or average assets (company basis). End losses = loans written off; provisions = the change in the stock of expected-loss provisions.
Ind AS buckets: performing, 30-90 days overdue and 90+ days overdue loans; ECL = expected-credit-loss provisions held against them. IRACP = the RBI's simpler minimum provisioning rules.
The annual re-estimation of default and loss rates (done in Q3); an overlay is an extra provision booked on management's judgement (₹852 cr in FY26).
Collections of the month's dues plus overdues ÷ the month's dues.

Profit ÷ average assets; profit ÷ average shareholders' equity.
New shares offered to existing shareholders pro rata; qualified institutions placement (shares sold to institutions).
Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India.
A Pacific warming pattern that often weakens India's monsoon; long-period average rainfall (the IMD's "normal").
Price ÷ book value per share. Justified P/B = (ROE − g) ÷ (cost of equity − g).
Book value plus the present value of future profit above the cost of equity.

AAA-rated (CRISIL, India Ratings, CARE); 44% of borrowings floating; public deposits ₹14,674 cr (11% of funding). A majority of economists expected a 25bp repo hike at the October-2026 RBI policy. We take +3bp in FY27E and +10bp more in FY28E.
assumptions._opexPctWhy: Operating expenses incl. depreciation and fees & commission expense ÷ average group AUM: 4.5% FY24, 4.3% FY25, 4.3% FY26; Q1FY27 annualised 4.3%. About 1pp of this is MIBL's commission payouts and DSA/sourcing costs (fees & commission expense ₹1,318 cr in FY26), which move with MIBL's fee income. Standalone opex is 2.7% of assets (FY26, Q1FY27) and management calls 2.5-2.7% 'a business model requirement'; headcount flat at ~22,600 while the book grows (Udaan digital stack). We allow 6bp a year of operating leverage.
assumptions._creditCostWhy: Provisions ÷ average group AUM: 3.7% FY22, 1.5% FY23, 2.0% FY24, 1.8% FY25 (flattered by a ₹434 cr release from the Q3FY25 ECL model refresh), 1.85% FY26 (incl. a ₹217 cr Q4 overlay; the ₹635 cr Q3 overlay only offset the ECL-refresh release). Q1FY27 1.57% annualised (company basis 1.5% of assets vs 1.9% in Q1FY26). Guidance: 1.3-1.7% of assets through the cycle, 'lower end if we execute well'. Against that, the 2026 monsoon ended ~12.6-13% below normal (fourth-weakest since 2001; UNI citing IMD, 30-Sep-2026) and tractors are 12% of AUM; after the last back-to-back deficient monsoons (2014: ~12% short; 2015: 86% of normal) ROE fell from 13% (FY16) to 8% (FY17) and profit 43% over FY15-17. We take 1.75% for FY27E and FY28E (≈1.6% on the company's asset basis; overlay of ₹852 cr kept, not released) and 1.65% in FY29E.
assumptions._taxRateWhy: FY26 effective 25.2% (₹965 cr on PBT ₹3,826 cr); FY25 25.3%.
assumptions._payoutWhy: DPS ₹7.50 for FY26 (375% of face value; ₹1,042 cr) = 36.5% of consolidated EPS ₹20.54 and 37% of standalone PAT; ₹6.50 for FY25 (38.5% of standalone profit after restatement), ₹6.30 for FY24. We keep 36%.
assumptions._minorityPctWhy: Minority share ₹6 cr of ₹2,861 cr FY26 profit (0.2%): Mahindra Ideal Finance (41.8% minority) and MRHFL (1.57%). MRHFL merges into MMFSL from 1-Apr-2027 (board approval 5-Aug-2026, swap 1.8 MMFSL shares per 10 MRHFL shares), so its minority falls away in FY28E-29E.
assumptions._otherIncomeWhy: Screener 'other income' = other income (₹81 cr FY26) + share of associates and JV (₹70 cr: Mahindra Manulife AMC 51% JV, Mahindra Finance USA 49%) less ~₹36 cr moved into revenue, plus exceptional items (−₹133 cr labour-code charge in Q3FY26). FY26 excluding the exceptional ₹116 cr; Q1FY27 ₹29 cr (run-rate ₹116 cr). We grow it with the AMC and US JV.
assumptions._capitalRaiseWhy: No raise: Tier 1 16.5% (Jun-2026) vs 10% minimum; MD: no capital needed 'in the next at least 6 to 8 quarters'; CFO comfortable taking debt/equity from 5.0x to '6-plus'. Last raise: ₹2,996 cr rights issue at ₹194 (1-for-8), allotted 9-Jun-2025.

valuation._why: Ke = 6.5% + 1.15 × 6% = 13.4% (house rf and ERP; beta 1.15 as for Shriram and Chola: a rural, cyclical vehicle lender whose profit fell 34-41% in FY17 and FY20-21; AAA funding argues for less, earnings volatility for more). sustainableRoe 14% = the top of the company's own record outside FY19 (FY23 11.7%, FY26 11.9% consolidated; standalone 14.3% annualised in Q1FY27) and roughly what the FY31 'ROA 2.2-2.5%' milestone gives at 5.5-6x leverage; it is above our FY27-29E path. g = 9% long-run book growth. Residual income fades ROE to 14% over 8 years; payout to 40% (FY26: 36.5%; the engine assumes no payout in the forecast years, see report).

methods.name: P/B
methods.why: The street's method (Motilal Oswal 2.0x Mar-28E book, HSBC 1.8x FY28E, Emkay 1.9x FY28E standalone book plus subsidiaries, Prabhudas Lilladher 1.5x FY28E adjusted book in a sum of the parts). 1.4x = own median forward P/B since Apr-2021 (1.4x) × listed-lender P/B move vs five-year medians (−6.4%, nine peers excluding M&M Finance) × regime 1.07 (median since Apr-2023, 1.5x, ÷ the full-window median, as in the other lender reports) = 1.40x. Our FY27-29E ROE (12.5-13.4%) is still below the 13.4% cost of equity, so we add no further premium for returns; scaling by our forecast ROE vs FY23-26 would give 1.5x (shown as a sensitivity only). Bull 1.8x = the highest forward P/B since 2021 (and HSBC's multiple); bear 1.1x = the FY22-23 median, about the 10th percentile since 2021.

methods.name: Justified P/B
methods.why: (ROE − g) ÷ (Ke − g) = (14 − 9) ÷ (13.4 − 9) on book at the 12-month target date.

methods.name: Residual income
methods.why: Book plus the present value of profit above the 13.4% cost of equity, ROE fading to 14%, rolled forward 6 months.

methods.name: P/E
methods.why: Cross-check only: 12x = own median forward P/E since Apr-2021 (12.7x; no trough years under the house rule) × listed-lender P/E move vs five-year medians (−15%, nine peers excluding M&M Finance) × regime 1.07 (median since Apr-2023, 13.6x, ÷ the full-window median) = 11.5x, rounded. Bull 13.6x = median since Apr-2023; bear 8.5x = lowest since 2021.

bull.label: Bull
bull.narrative: The transformation pays off: AUM +17/18/18% (inside the 16-18% aspiration) as tractors, used vehicles, SME and mortgages all grow; IRDAI's caps are softened (fees ~1.9% of AUM); opex falls faster on the digital stack; credit cost ~1.4-1.45% of AUM (lower end of guidance) as the monsoon damage stays contained and the ₹852 cr overlay is not needed; ROA heads to 2.5% and long-run ROE to 16%.

bear.label: Bear
bear.narrative: A rural down-cycle like FY16-17 or FY20-21: the weak 2026 monsoon and a second poor year hit tractor and small-transport borrowers; AUM +10/11/11%, credit cost back to ~2.3-2.4% of AUM (FY24-26 average plus the drought), funding 20bp dearer, most loan-linked insurance commission capped away; ROE falls back to ~8.5-9% and long-run ROE to 11%.
